claim: GPCRs represent one-third of clinically prescribed drugs.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) play crucial roles in the regulation of a wide variety of physiological processes and represent one-third of clinically prescribed drugs (Hauser et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hauser et al., 2017

claim: Gα proteins are divided into four major families (Gs, Gi/o, Gq/11, and G12/13) encoded by 16 human genes.
source: Gα proteins are divided into four major families (Gs, Gi/o, Gq/11, and G12/13) encoded by 16 human genes.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about G protein classification

claim: Many GPCRs can couple to more than one G protein family.
source: It has now become evident that many GPCRs can couple to more than one G protein family and that ligands can selectively promote the activation of different subsets of these pathways (Namkung et al., 2018; Quoyer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Namkung et al., 2018 and Quoyer et al., 2013

claim: Ligands can selectively promote the activation of different subsets of G protein pathways.
source: It has now become evident that many GPCRs can couple to more than one G protein family and that ligands can selectively promote the activation of different subsets of these pathways (Namkung et al., 2018; Quoyer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Namkung et al., 2018 and Quoyer et al., 2013

claim: The concept of ligand-biased signaling was first established for ligand-directed selectivity between βarrestin and G protein.
source: These observations extended the concept of ligand-biased signaling, which was first established for ligand-directed selectivity between βarrestin and G protein (Azzi et al., 2003; Wei et al., 2003), to functional selectivity between G proteins.
evidence: Supported by citations to Azzi et al., 2003 and Wei et al., 2003

claim: Ligand-directed functional selectivity offers the opportunity of activating pathways important for therapeutic efficacy while minimizing activation of pathways responsible for undesirable side effects.
source: Ligand-directed functional selectivity represents a promising avenue for GPCRs drug discovery since it offers the opportunity of activating pathways important for therapeutic efficacy while minimizing activation of pathways responsible for undesirable side effects (Galandrin et al., 2007; Kenakin, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Galandrin et al., 2007 and Kenakin, 2019

claim: EMTA biosensors monitor the translocation of downstream effectors to the plasma membrane for Gi/o, Gq/11, and G12/13.
source: The platform includes 15 pathway-selective enhanced bystander bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (ebBRET) biosensors monitoring the translocation of downstream effectors to the plasma membrane for Gi/o, Gq/11, and G12/13, the dissociation of the Gα subunit from the plasma membrane for Gs and the recruitment of βarrestin to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Description of the experimental platform developed in this study

claim: EMTA biosensors monitor the dissociation of the Gα subunit from the plasma membrane for Gs.
source: The platform includes 15 pathway-selective enhanced bystander bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (ebBRET) biosensors monitoring the translocation of downstream effectors to the plasma membrane for Gi/o, Gq/11, and G12/13, the dissociation of the Gα subunit from the plasma membrane for Gs and the recruitment of βarrestin to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Description of the experimental platform developed in this study

claim: EMTA biosensors monitor the recruitment of βarrestin to the plasma membrane.
source: The platform includes 15 pathway-selective enhanced bystander bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (ebBRET) biosensors monitoring the translocation of downstream effectors to the plasma membrane for Gi/o, Gq/11, and G12/13, the dissociation of the Gα subunit from the plasma membrane for Gs and the recruitment of βarrestin to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Description of the experimental platform developed in this study

claim: EMTA does not require modification of receptors or G proteins (except for Gs).
source: Unlike most of the existing detection systems, EMTA does not require modification of receptors or G proteins (except for Gs).
evidence: Description of the experimental platform developed in this study

claim: EMTA is suitable for the detection of constitutive activity.
source: EMTA was found to be suitable for the detection of constitutive activity, inverse agonism, biased signaling and polypharmacology.
evidence: Experimental validation presented in the study

claim: EMTA is suitable for the detection of inverse agonism.
source: EMTA was found to be suitable for the detection of constitutive activity, inverse agonism, biased signaling and polypharmacology.
evidence: Experimental validation presented in the study

claim: EMTA is suitable for the detection of biased signaling.
source: EMTA was found to be suitable for the detection of constitutive activity, inverse agonism, biased signaling and polypharmacology.
evidence: Experimental validation presented in the study

claim: EMTA is suitable for the detection of polypharmacology.
source: EMTA was found to be suitable for the detection of constitutive activity, inverse agonism, biased signaling and polypharmacology.
evidence: Experimental validation presented in the study

claim: Profiling of 100 therapeutically relevant human GPCRs resulted in 1500 pathway-specific concentration-response curves.
source: Profiling of 100 therapeutically relevant human GPCRs resulted in 1500 pathway-specific concentration-response curves and revealed a great diversity of coupling profiles ranging from exquisite selectivity to broad promiscuity.
evidence: Quantitative description of experimental results

claim: The profiling revealed a great diversity of coupling profiles ranging from exquisite selectivity to broad promiscuity.
source: Profiling of 100 therapeutically relevant human GPCRs resulted in 1500 pathway-specific concentration-response curves and revealed a great diversity of coupling profiles ranging from exquisite selectivity to broad promiscuity.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from the study

claim: Upon GPCR activation, RlucII-tagged effectors translocate to the plasma membrane to bind activated Gα proteins, bringing RlucII in close proximity to rGFP-CAAX, leading to an increase in ebBRET.
source: Upon GPCR activation, the energy donor-fused effectors translocate to the plasma membrane to bind activated Gα proteins, bringing RlucII in close proximity to the energy acceptor, Renilla green fluorescent protein, targeted to the plasma membrane through a CAAX motif (rGFP-CAAX), thus leading to an increase in ebBRET.
evidence: Description of the biosensor mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Gαs dissociates from the plasma membrane following its activation.
source: Because no selective soluble downstream effector of Gs exists, the assay was modified taking advantage of Gαs dissociation from the plasma membrane following its activation (Wedegaertner et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wedegaertner et al., 1996

claim: Activation of Gαs upon GPCR stimulation leads to its dissociation from the plasma membrane, resulting in a reduction in ebBRET.
source: Its activation upon GPCR stimulation leads to its dissociation from the plasma membrane (Martin and Lambert, 2016), resulting in a reduction in ebBRET (Figure 1B, bottom).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martin and Lambert, 2016, and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: The dopamine-promoted increase in ebBRET between Rap1GAP-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX in the presence of Gαi/o subunits was not affected by the Gq/11-selective inhibitor UBO-QIC.
source: The dopamine-promoted increase in ebBRET between Rap1GAP-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX in the presence of Gαi/o subunits was not affected by the Gq/11-selective inhibitor UBO-QIC (a.k.a., FR900359; Schrage et al., 2015; Figure 2A, left)
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating pharmacological selectivity

claim: The Gαi/o family inhibitor pertussis toxin (PTX) completely blocked the response for all members of Gαi/o family except for Gαz.
source: whereas the Gαi/o family inhibitor, pertussis toxin (PTX), completely blocked the response for all members of Gαi/o family except for Gαz, known to be insensitive to PTX (Casey et al., 1990; Figure 2A, right).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2A, with citation to Casey et al., 1990 for Gαz PTX insensitivity

claim: Gαz is insensitive to PTX.
source: whereas the Gαi/o family inhibitor, pertussis toxin (PTX), completely blocked the response for all members of Gαi/o family except for Gαz, known to be insensitive to PTX (Casey et al., 1990; Figure 2A, right).
evidence: Supported by citation to Casey et al., 1990

claim: GnRH stimulation of the GnRH receptor promoted ebBRET between p63-RhoGEF-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX in the presence of different Gαq/11 subunits.
source: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) stimulation of the GnRH receptor (GnRHR), used as a prototypical Gq/11-coupled receptor, promoted ebBRET between the RlucII-fused Gq/11 binding domain of p63-RhoGEF (p63-RhoGEF-RlucII; Lutz et al., 2007; Rojas et al., 2007) and rGFP-CAAX.
evidence: Experimental data with citations to Lutz et al., 2007 and Rojas et al., 2007 for the p63-RhoGEF binding domain

claim: The ebBRET increase observed in the presence of different Gαq/11 subunits was not significantly affected by PTX.
source: The ebBRET increase observed in the presence of different Gαq/11 subunits was not significantly (p = 0.077, 0.0636 and 0.073 for Gq, G11, and G14, respectively) affected by PTX (Figure 2B, right)
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: UBO-QIC completely blocked the response for all members of Gαq/11 family except for Gα15.
source: whereas UBO-QIC completely blocked the response for all members of Gαq/11 family except for Gα15, known to be insensitive to UBO-QIC (Schrage et al., 2015; Figure 2B, left).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2B, with citation to Schrage et al., 2015 for Gα15 UBO-QIC insensitivity

claim: Gα15 is insensitive to UBO-QIC.
source: whereas UBO-QIC completely blocked the response for all members of Gαq/11 family except for Gα15, known to be insensitive to UBO-QIC (Schrage et al., 2015; Figure 2B, left).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schrage et al., 2015

claim: Deletion of Gi/o or Gq/11 subtypes completely abolished the responses induced by D2 or GnRHR activation in the absence of heterologously expressed G proteins.
source: These two G protein-specific EMTA were sensitive enough to detect responses elicited by endogenous G proteins since deletion of Gi/o (ΔGi/o) or Gq/11 (ΔGq/11) subtypes completely abolished the responses induced by D2 or GnRHR activation in the absence of heterologously expressed G proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I using knockout cell lines

claim: WIN-55,212–2-promoted ebBRET between PDZ-RhoGEF-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX in the presence of Gα12 or Gα13 was not affected by UBO-QIC.
source: The ebBRET between PDZ-RhoGEF-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX in the presence of Gα12 or Gα13 promoted by the cannabinoid agonist WIN-55,212–2 was not affected by UBO-QIC (Figure 2C, top left)
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating pharmacological selectivity

claim: WIN-55,212–2-promoted ebBRET between PDZ-RhoGEF-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX in the presence of Gα12 or Gα13 was not affected by PTX.
source: The ebBRET between PDZ-RhoGEF-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX in the presence of Gα12 or Gα13 promoted by the cannabinoid agonist WIN-55,212–2 was not affected by UBO-QIC (Figure 2C, top left), nor PTX (Figure 2C, top right).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating pharmacological selectivity

claim: PDZ-RhoGEF-RlucII/rGFP-CAAX ebBRET was observed only following reintroduction of either Gα12 or Gα13 in ΔG12/13 cells.
source: As expected, PDZ-RhoGEF-RlucII/rGFP-CAAX ebBRET was observed only following reintroduction of either Gα12 (ΔG12/13_+G12) or Gα13 (ΔG12/13_+G13) (Figure 2C, bottom left).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C using knockout cell lines with rescue

claim: The G12/13 coupling of CB1 was confirmed by monitoring the recruitment of PKN to the plasma membrane.
source: The G12/13 coupling of CB1 was further confirmed by monitoring the recruitment of PKN to the plasma membrane (Figure 2C, bottom right) in agreement with previous reports (Inoue et al., 2019).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C, with citation to Inoue et al., 2019

claim: Only over-expression of the Gα family members corresponding to their selective effectors significantly increased the recruitment of the effector-RlucII to the plasma membrane for the ETA receptor.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, only over-expression of the Gα family members corresponding to their selective effectors (Rap1GAP for Gi/o, p63-RhoGEF for Gq/11, and PDZ-RhoGEF for G12/13) significantly increased the recruitment of the effector-RlucII to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 demonstrating effector selectivity

claim: Competition with endogenous G proteins did not occur to a significant extent in the heterologous expression configuration.
source: It should be noted that in the heterologous expression configuration, competition with endogenous G proteins did not occur to a significant extent since the potencies of the responses to a given G protein subtype were not affected by genetic deletion of the different G protein family members (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1A

claim: Overexpression of G proteins, GPCRs or effectors-RlucII did not affect the potencies of the responses observed.
source: Similarly, overexpression of G proteins, GPCRs or effectors-RlucII did not affect the potencies of the responses observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1B-D)
evidence: Analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1B-D

claim: EMTA allows imaging of the real-time recruitment of the G protein effectors to the plasma membrane.
source: In addition to spectrometric assessment of coupling selectivity (above) and activation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), EMTA allows to image the real-time recruitment of the G protein effectors to the plasma membrane (Videos 1–3) thus providing spatiotemporal resolution for the imaging detection of Gαi/o, Gαq/11, and Gα12/13 activation.
evidence: Demonstrated by Videos 1–3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: EMTA provides spatiotemporal resolution for the imaging detection of Gαi/o, Gαq/11, and Gα12/13 activation.
source: In addition to spectrometric assessment of coupling selectivity (above) and activation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), EMTA allows to image the real-time recruitment of the G protein effectors to the plasma membrane (Videos 1–3) thus providing spatiotemporal resolution for the imaging detection of Gαi/o, Gαq/11, and Gα12/13 activation.
evidence: Demonstrated by Videos 1–3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: EMTA shows significantly larger assay windows compared to BRET assays based on Gαβγ dissociation for the 6 Gα subunits tested for eight selected receptors.
source: The sensitivity of the EMTA platform is illustrated by a direct side-by-side comparison of the signals detected with EMTA vs. BRET assays based on Gαβγ dissociation (Gαβγ) (Galés et al., 2005; Galés et al., 2006; Olsen et al., 2020), that reveals a significantly larger assay windows for EMTA for the 6 Gα subunits tested for eight selected receptors, (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Comparative experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5, with citations to Galés et al., 2005, 2006, and Olsen et al., 2020

claim: Lithocholic acid stimulation resulted in a concentration-dependent decrease in ebBRET between Gαs-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX.
source: As expected, lithocholic acid stimulation resulted in a concentration-dependent decrease in ebBRET between Gαs-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX (Figure 2D, left).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Cholera toxin (CTX) led to a decrease in ebBRET between Gαs-RlucII and rGFP-CAAX.
source: Cholera toxin (CTX), which directly activates Gαs (De Haan and Hirst, 2004), led to a decrease in ebBRET (Figure 2D, center)
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2D, with citation to De Haan and Hirst, 2004 for CTX mechanism

claim: Loss of Gαs plasma membrane localization results from its activation.
source: Cholera toxin (CTX), which directly activates Gαs (De Haan and Hirst, 2004), led to a decrease in ebBRET (Figure 2D, center), confirming that loss of Gαs plasma membrane localization results from its activation.
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The potency of lithocholic acid to promote Gs dissociation from the plasma membrane was well in line with its potency to increase cAMP production.
source: The potency of lithocholic acid to promote Gs dissociation from the plasma membrane was well in line with its potency to increase cAMP production as assessed using a BRET²-based EPAC biosensor (Leduc et al., 2009; Figure 2D, right).
evidence: Comparative experimental data shown in Figure 2D, with citation to Leduc et al., 2009 for the EPAC biosensor

claim: The Gs-plasma membrane dissociation ebBRET signal was not affected by UBO-QIC or PTX.
source: The Gs-plasma membrane dissociation ebBRET signal was not affected by UBO-QIC or PTX (Figure 2D, left), confirming the selectivity of the biosensor.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2D demonstrating pharmacological selectivity

claim: The study assessed the signaling signature of a panel of 100 human GPCRs that are either already the target of clinically used drugs (74 receptors), considered for pre- or clinical drug development (6 receptors), or pathophysiologically relevant.
source: We used EMTA to assess the signaling signature of a panel of 100 human GPCRs that are either already the target of clinically used drugs (74 receptors), considered for pre- or clinical drug development (6 receptors), or pathophysiologically relevant (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Description of the receptor panel used in the study

claim: The study quantified the ability of each receptor to activate 15 pathways: Gαs, Gαi1, Gαi2, GαoA, GαoB, Gαz, Gα12, Gα13, Gαq, Gα11, Gα14, Gα15 and βarrestin 2 as well as βarrestin 1 and 2 in the presence of GRK2.
source: To establish the coupling potentials for each receptor, we quantified its ability to activate 15 pathways: Gαs, Gαi1, Gαi2, GαoA, GαoB, Gαz, Gα12, Gα13, Gαq, Gα11, Gα14, Gα15 and βarrestin 2 as well as βarrestin 1 and 2 in the presence of GRK2 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Description of the experimental approach

claim: 29% of the receptors coupled to only one G protein family.
source: In our dataset, which is the first using unmodified GPCRs and Gα proteins (except for Gs), 29% of the receptors coupled to only one family, whereas others displayed more promiscuity by coupling to 2, 3, or 4 families (36%, 25%, and 10%, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 36% of the receptors coupled to 2 G protein families.
source: In our dataset, which is the first using unmodified GPCRs and Gα proteins (except for Gs), 29% of the receptors coupled to only one family, whereas others displayed more promiscuity by coupling to 2, 3, or 4 families (36%, 25%, and 10%, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 25% of the receptors coupled to 3 G protein families.
source: In our dataset, which is the first using unmodified GPCRs and Gα proteins (except for Gs), 29% of the receptors coupled to only one family, whereas others displayed more promiscuity by coupling to 2, 3, or 4 families (36%, 25%, and 10%, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 10% of the receptors coupled to 4 G protein families.
source: In our dataset, which is the first using unmodified GPCRs and Gα proteins (except for Gs), 29% of the receptors coupled to only one family, whereas others displayed more promiscuity by coupling to 2, 3, or 4 families (36%, 25%, and 10%, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 27% of the receptors coupling to Gi/o only activated this subtype family.
source: Indeed, 27% of the receptors coupling to Gi/o only activated this subtype family in comparison to 0, 2.4 and 9.1% for receptors activating G12/13, Gq/11, and Gs, respectively, thus displaying more promiscuous coupling.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 0% of the receptors coupling to G12/13 only activated this subtype family.
source: Indeed, 27% of the receptors coupling to Gi/o only activated this subtype family in comparison to 0, 2.4 and 9.1% for receptors activating G12/13, Gq/11, and Gs, respectively, thus displaying more promiscuous coupling.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 2.4% of the receptors coupling to Gq/11 only activated this subtype family.
source: Indeed, 27% of the receptors coupling to Gi/o only activated this subtype family in comparison to 0, 2.4 and 9.1% for receptors activating G12/13, Gq/11, and Gs, respectively, thus displaying more promiscuous coupling.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 9.1% of the receptors coupling to Gs only activated this subtype family.
source: Indeed, 27% of the receptors coupling to Gi/o only activated this subtype family in comparison to 0, 2.4 and 9.1% for receptors activating G12/13, Gq/11, and Gs, respectively, thus displaying more promiscuous coupling.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 89% of the tested receptors activate a Gi/o family member.
source: When examining the frequency of coupling for each Gα subunit family (Figure 4C), the Gi/o family members were the most commonly activated, with 89% of the tested receptors activating a Gi/o family member.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: 33% of the receptors activate Gs family members.
source: In contrast, only 33%, 49%, and 45% of the receptors activate Gs, G12/13, or Gq/11 (excluding Gα15) family members, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 49% of the receptors activate G12/13 family members.
source: In contrast, only 33%, 49%, and 45% of the receptors activate Gs, G12/13, or Gq/11 (excluding Gα15) family members, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 45% of the receptors activate Gq/11 (excluding Gα15) family members.
source: In contrast, only 33%, 49%, and 45% of the receptors activate Gs, G12/13, or Gq/11 (excluding Gα15) family members, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: Gα15 was found to be activated by 81% of the receptors.
source: Not surprisingly, and consistent with its reported promiscuous coupling, Gα15 was found to be activated by 81% of the receptors.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 33% of Gi/o-coupled receptors can couple to only a subpopulation of the Gi/o family.
source: For instance, 33% of Gi/o-coupled receptors can couple to only a subpopulation of the family (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: For the Gq/11 family, only 44% activate all family members.
source: For the Gq/11 family, only 44% activate all family members with 45% activating only Gα15 and 11% engaging only two or three members of the family.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 45% of Gq/11-coupled receptors activate only Gα15.
source: For the Gq/11 family, only 44% activate all family members with 45% activating only Gα15 and 11% engaging only two or three members of the family.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: 11% of Gq/11-coupled receptors engage only two or three members of the family.
source: For the Gq/11 family, only 44% activate all family members with 45% activating only Gα15 and 11% engaging only two or three members of the family.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: The serotonin 5-HT2B receptor activates only GαoB and Gαz.
source: A striking example of intra-family coupling selectivity is the serotonin 5-HT2B that activates only GαoB and Gαz and GPR65 that selectively activates GαoB.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: GPR65 selectively activates GαoB.
source: A striking example of intra-family coupling selectivity is the serotonin 5-HT2B that activates only GαoB and Gαz and GPR65 that selectively activates GαoB.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: Histamine H2 and MC3R receptors show preferred activation of GαoB and Gαz.
source: Similarly, when considering the ligand-promoted responses above our threshold criteria (see Materials and methods), histamine H2 and MC3R receptors show preferred activation of GαoB and Gαz, whereas the prostaglandin F (FP) and neuropeptide Y5 (Y5) receptors preferentially activate GαoB, GαoA, and Gαz.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: The prostaglandin F (FP) and neuropeptide Y5 (Y5) receptors preferentially activate GαoB, GαoA, and Gαz.
source: Similarly, when considering the ligand-promoted responses above our threshold criteria (see Materials and methods), histamine H2 and MC3R receptors show preferred activation of GαoB and Gαz, whereas the prostaglandin F (FP) and neuropeptide Y5 (Y5) receptors preferentially activate GαoB, GαoA, and Gαz.
evidence: Experimental data from the study

claim: 22% of receptors did not recruit βarrestin 1 or 2, even in the presence of overexpressed GRK2.
source: When considering βarrestin recruitment, our analysis shows that 22% of receptors did not recruit βarrestin 1 or 2, even in the presence of overexpressed GRK2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Among the receptors able to recruit βarrestins, only 1.3% selectively recruited βarrestin1.
source: Among the receptors able to recruit βarrestins, only a very small number selectively recruited βarrestin1 (1.3%) or βarrestin2 (6.4%), most of them recruiting both βarrestins in the presence of GRK2 (92.3%) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Among the receptors able to recruit βarrestins, 6.4% selectively recruited βarrestin2.
source: Among the receptors able to recruit βarrestins, only a very small number selectively recruited βarrestin1 (1.3%) or βarrestin2 (6.4%), most of them recruiting both βarrestins in the presence of GRK2 (92.3%) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: 92.3% of receptors able to recruit βarrestins recruited both βarrestins in the presence of GRK2.
source: Among the receptors able to recruit βarrestins, only a very small number selectively recruited βarrestin1 (1.3%) or βarrestin2 (6.4%), most of them recruiting both βarrestins in the presence of GRK2 (92.3%) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Overexpression of GRK2 potentiated the recruitment of βarrestin2 for 68% of receptors.
source: Overexpression of GRK2 potentiated the recruitment of βarrestin2 for 68% of receptors highlighting the importance of GRK2 expression level in determining βarrestin activation (Supplementary files 3 and 2).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of experimental data from the study

claim: There is 64% identity of couplings between the EMTA and Inoue's datasets.
source: Altogether, the comparative analysis reveals 64% and 69% identity of couplings between the EMTA and Inoue's or GtP datasets, respectively.
evidence: Comparative analysis of datasets

claim: There is 69% identity of couplings between the EMTA and GtP datasets.
source: Altogether, the comparative analysis reveals 64% and 69% identity of couplings between the EMTA and Inoue's or GtP datasets, respectively.
evidence: Comparative analysis of datasets

claim: Ligand stimulation of FP and CysLT2 receptors led to Rho and ezrin activation that were insensitive to the Gq/11 inhibitor YM-254890.
source: Ligand stimulation of FP and CysLT2 receptors led to Rho and ezrin activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), that were insensitive to the Gq/11 inhibitor YM-254890, confirming that these receptors activate Gα12/13.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A

claim: FP and CysLT2 receptors activate Gα12/13.
source: Ligand stimulation of FP and CysLT2 receptors led to Rho and ezrin activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), that were insensitive to the Gq/11 inhibitor YM-254890, confirming that these receptors activate Gα12/13.
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A

claim: Expression of Gα15 significantly increased the PGE2-promoted calcium response in EP2 receptor-expressing cells.
source: For prostaglandin E2 (EP2) and κ-opioid (κOR) receptors, which couple to G15 but no other Gq/11 members, expression of Gα15 significantly increased the PGE2- and Dynorphin A- promoted calcium responses.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: Expression of Gα15 significantly increased the Dynorphin A-promoted calcium response in κOR receptor-expressing cells.
source: For prostaglandin E2 (EP2) and κ-opioid (κOR) receptors, which couple to G15 but no other Gq/11 members, expression of Gα15 significantly increased the PGE2- and Dynorphin A- promoted calcium responses.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: Treatment with YM-254890 completely abolished the agonist-promoted calcium response in α2AAR and V2 receptors in the absence of Gα15.
source: For α2A adrenergic (α2AAR) and vasopressin 2 (V2) receptors that couple other Gq/11 family members, treatment with YM-254890 completely abolished the agonist-promoted calcium response in the absence of Gα15.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: The calcium response evoked by α2AAR and V2 agonists following Gα15 expression was completely insensitive to YM-254890.
source: In contrast, the calcium response evoked by α2AAR and V2 agonists following Gα15 expression was completely insensitive to YM-254890 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B), confirming that these receptors can activate this YM-254890-insensitive G protein subtype (Takasaki et al., 2004).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, with citation to Takasaki et al., 2004

claim: Transfection of increasing amounts of adenosine A1 receptor led to a receptor-dependent increase in basal ebBRET of the Gαi2-activation sensor.
source: Transfection of increasing amounts of adenosine A1 receptor (A1) led to a receptor-dependent increase in basal ebBRET of the Gαi2-activation sensor (Figure 5A, left), reflecting A1 constitutive activity.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The A1 inverse agonist DPCPX dose-dependently decreased the constitutive A1-mediated activation of Gαi2.
source: The A1 inverse agonist DPCPX (Lu et al., 2014) dose-dependently decreased the constitutive A1-mediated activation of Gαi2 (Figure 5A, left), indicating that EMTA can detect inverse agonism.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5A, with citation to Lu et al., 2014

claim: EMTA can detect inverse agonism.
source: The A1 inverse agonist DPCPX (Lu et al., 2014) dose-dependently decreased the constitutive A1-mediated activation of Gαi2 (Figure 5A, left), indicating that EMTA can detect inverse agonism.
evidence: Inference from experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Increased CB1 expression led to a ligand-independent constitutive activation of Gz.

claim: The CB1 inverse agonist rimonabant completely blocked the constitutive activation of Gz by CB1.
source: As illustrated in Figure 5A (right), increase CB1 expression led to a ligand-independent constitutive activation of Gz, that could be completely blocked by the CB1 inverse agonist rimonabant.

claim: Angiotensin analogs SII, saralasin or TRV027 displayed biased signaling by promoting efficient βarrestin2 recruitment but marginal or no Gαq, Gαi2, or Gα13 activation as compared to angiotensin II.

claim: Angiotensin II activated all G proteins (Gαq, Gαi2, Gα13) and βarrestin2.

claim: Two naturally occurring variants of human GPR17 (isoform 2) localized in the TM3 E/DRY motif resulted in altered functional selectivity profiles.

claim: The Asp128Asn variant of GPR17 displayed WT-like activity on Gαi2 but lost the ability to activate Gαq and βarrestin2.
source: Whereas the Asp128Asn variant displayed WT-like activity on Gαi2, it lost the ability to activate Gαq and βarrestin2.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The Arg129His variant of GPR17 resulted in an increased constitutive βarrestin2 recruitment and a loss of Gαi2 and Gαq protein signaling.

claim: 95% of receptors activate either Gαz (73%) or Gα15 (81%).

claim: The Gz/G15 sensor captured the activation of 24 GPCRs in a safety panel.

claim: Dopamine and serotonin activate the α2AAR.

claim: Noradrenaline and serotonin activate the D2 receptor.

claim: EMTA provides direct real-time measurement of proximal signaling events following GPCR activation.
source: First, EMTA provides direct real-time measurement of proximal signaling events following GPCR activation (i.e. Gα protein activation and βarrestin recruitment) and resulting in lower level of amplification than those of assays relying on enzymatic activity of downstream effectors (i.e.: adenylyl cyclase or phospholipase C) or artificial detection systems (i.e.: gene-reporter or TGF-α shedding assays) that measure signal accumulation sometimes following extended incubation times.
evidence: Description of the advantages of the EMTA platform
